objectives: Describe the systolic-array structure of TPUs.
Reason about the roofline performance model.

slides.title: GPU architecture: SMs + tensor cores
slides.body:
**GPU (Graphics Processing Unit)**: massively parallel processor originally designed for graphics; now dominant for ML.

**NVIDIA H100 example** (2022 architecture):
- 132 **Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs)** — units of execution.
- Each SM has: 4 sub-warps × 32 threads = 128 'CUDA cores' (FP32) + 4 tensor cores + shared memory + register file.
- Total: 16,896 FP32 cores + 528 tensor cores.
- 80 GB HBM3 @ 3.35 TB/s.
- 60 TFLOPs FP32, 1000 TFLOPs FP16 via tensor cores, 4000 TOPS INT8.

**SIMT execution**: Single Instruction, Multiple Thread. Groups of 32 threads ('warps') execute the same instruction in lock-step. Diverging branches serialize the warp (slow path).

**Memory hierarchy**:
- Registers (per thread): fast, plentiful.
- Shared memory / L1 (per SM): ~228 KB. Programmable scratchpad.
- L2 cache (chip-wide): ~50 MB. Shared.
- HBM: GBs.

**Tensor cores**: dedicated matrix-multiply units. A single tensor-core instruction performs a 4×4×4 matrix multiply-accumulate in 1 cycle (and more in newer generations). Specialized for ML.

**Modern tensor types**:
- FP32 / FP16 / BF16 (brain float, wider range than FP16).
- FP8 (Hopper / Blackwell): 8-bit float with E5M2 or E4M3 formats.
- INT8 / INT4 for inference quantization.
- Sparsity: 2:4 structured sparsity (skip half the multiplies).

**CUDA programming**: write 'kernels' as C++ functions; launch with grid of thread blocks. Each thread has a unique (block, thread) ID. The CUDA runtime + hardware schedule warps on SMs.

**Other GPUs**:
- AMD MI300: similar architecture, ROCm software stack.
- Intel Gaudi 2/3: matrix engines + general-purpose tensors.
- Apple GPU (M-series): unified memory; smaller scale; tile-based deferred renderer for graphics.
- Mobile GPUs (Mali, Adreno, PowerVR): tile-based for power efficiency.

slides.title: TPU + systolic arrays
slides.body:
**Google TPU (Tensor Processing Unit)**: custom ASIC for ML, used in Google data centers + Cloud. Architecture distinct from GPUs.

**Core: systolic array**. A 2D grid of multiply-accumulate (MAC) units, each connected to neighbors. Data flows through the grid systematically.

**TPUv4 example**:
- 128 × 128 systolic array per core. 16,384 MACs.
- BF16 / INT8 supported.
- 32 GB HBM per chip.
- ~275 TFLOPs BF16, ~275 TOPS INT8 per chip.
- Massively multi-chip (TPUv4 pod: 4096 chips with optical interconnect, ~1 ExaFLOP).

**Systolic-array operation**:
1. Weight matrix W is loaded into the array (each MAC holds one weight).
2. Activations stream in from the LEFT, one column per cycle.
3. Partial products accumulate vertically.
4. After N cycles (where N is matrix dimension), output emerges from the right.

**Why it's efficient**:
- Each MAC reuses the weight ~N times.
- Each activation reuses ~N times.
- Massive data reuse → much less memory traffic than naive matrix multiply.
- Simple control: neighbor-to-neighbor data movement, no global routing.

**Trade-offs vs GPU**:
- ✅ More efficient (less area, less power per MAC) for matrix-multiply-heavy workloads.
- ✅ Higher utilization (~70-80%) on big matrix multiplies.
- ❌ Inflexible for general workloads.
- ❌ Tail effects: small matrices waste the array.

**Other ML accelerators**:
- **Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine**: an entire wafer = one chip. 850K cores, 40 GB on-chip SRAM. Targets large-model training.
- **Graphcore IPU**: massive on-chip SRAM (~900 MB), MIMD architecture.
- **Tenstorrent Wormhole**: similar to IPU; scales out via direct chip-to-chip Ethernet.
- **AWS Trainium / Inferentia**: in-house Amazon ML chips.
- **Apple Neural Engine**: mobile/edge inference (~38 TOPS in M3).
- **Edge TPU / Coral / Hailo**: low-power inference.

slides.title: Roofline model + the FLOPs/byte arithmetic intensity
slides.body:
The **roofline model** (Williams 2009): a simple, predictive model of HW performance limits.

**Arithmetic intensity (AI)**: FLOPs per byte of memory traffic. Units: FLOPs/byte.
- Matrix multiply: ~2N FLOPs per element. AI grows with N. Good for hardware.
- Vector ops: 1 FLOP per element × ~4 bytes = 0.25 FLOPs/byte. Memory-bound.
- BLAS-3 routines (gemm): high AI, compute-bound.
- BLAS-1/-2 routines (axpy, gemv): low AI, memory-bound.

**Roofline**:
$$\text{Performance} = \min(\text{Peak FLOPS}, \text{AI} \times \text{Peak Bandwidth})$$

Plot AI on x-axis (log), achievable FLOPS on y-axis (log):
- Below 'ridge point': bandwidth-bound. Performance = AI × BW.
- Above 'ridge point': compute-bound. Performance = peak FLOPS.

**Modern hardware ridge points** (FLOPS/byte at which compute saturates):
- Apple M-series CPU: ~10 FLOPS/byte.
- NVIDIA H100 FP16: 1000 / 3.35 TB/s ≈ ~300 FLOPS/byte.
- TPU v4 BF16: 275 TFLOPS / 1.2 TB/s ≈ ~230 FLOPS/byte.
- AMD Genoa CPU: ~5 FLOPS/byte.

High ridge point = the hardware needs HIGH AI workloads to use compute. ML matrix multiply has AI ~100-1000 (large matrices), staying compute-bound. Vector or low-batch-size inference has AI <10, becoming bandwidth-bound + leaving compute idle.

**Implications**:
- Lower-precision data (FP8, INT8) doubles AI (smaller bytes per op).
- Operator fusion (combine multiple ops into one kernel) increases AI by reusing values.
- KV-cache + tiling improves AI in attention.
- Memory bandwidth (HBM > GDDR > DDR > NVMe) directly determines bandwidth-bound performance.

**Industry frontier**:
- More aggressive low-precision (FP4, FP6 experimental).
- Sparse training/inference (skip zero or near-zero weights).
- Mixture-of-experts (route to subset of weights per token; effectively higher AI per active parameter).
- On-package + 3D-stacked memory (closer = higher bandwidth = lower ridge point).

question.question: Apply roofline to a matrix multiplication
question.goal: GPU peak: 100 TFLOPS FP16, 1 TB/s HBM. Run matrix multiply A (1024×1024) × B (1024×1024) = C (1024×1024). Each element of C requires 1024 multiply-adds.

steps.prompt: Memory traffic: read A + B + write C = 3 × 1024² × 2 bytes (FP16) = ?
steps.reveal: ~6 MB (assuming each matrix read once + each output written once).
~340 FLOPs/byte. Above this hardware's ridge point (100 / 1 = 100 FLOPs/byte). COMPUTE-BOUND.

~22 μs. At memory bandwidth limit: 6.29e6 / 1e12 = 6.3 μs (memory could finish faster). So compute is the binding constraint. Real-world GEMM often hits ~80% of peak (overhead + tail effects) → ~28 μs.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{Roofline: } \text{Performance} = \min(\text{Peak}, \text{AI} \times \text{BW})}$$ Roofline is the ML engineer's mental model. Large GEMM (high AI) = compute-bound = scale with FLOPS. Small batch attention or vector ops (low AI) = bandwidth-bound = scale with bandwidth. Optimization strategies depend on which regime: compute-bound → use lower precision (more FLOPS/byte effectively); bandwidth-bound → fuse ops to reduce memory traffic, use more on-chip cache.

question.question: Google TPUs use systolic arrays while NVIDIA GPUs use SIMT cores + tensor cores. Trade-offs?
options: TPU: more efficient on big GEMMs (high utilization, less control overhead), less flexible for general code. GPU: more flexible, slightly less efficient per GEMM but handles smaller batches + irregular workloads better.
question.explanation: Systolic arrays are HIGHLY specialized for matrix multiply. ~70-80% utilization on big GEMM, but small matrices waste the array. GPUs are more general-purpose: tensor cores boost matrix multiply, but the surrounding general SIMT cores handle the rest. Trade-off: TPU wins on pure transformer training at scale; GPU wins on diverse workloads (mixed precision, irregular shapes, custom ops). Both architectures evolved; GPUs added more tensor functionality; TPUs added more flexibility around the array. Both essential in modern ML.

slides.workedSolution: Strength: 70-80% utilization on big GEMM, minimal control overhead, every cycle does useful work. Weakness: rigid shape; small matrices waste array; non-GEMM ops (activations, norms, softmax) require auxiliary units; flexibility costs efficiency. GPU SMs are softer; less peak efficiency but better at irregular workloads. NVIDIA + Google compete + co-evolve; modern systems use mixes.

question.question: Tensor core does 4×4×4 FP16 matrix multiply-accumulate per cycle. At 1 GHz that's how many TFLOPS per tensor core?
Choosing an accelerator
question.prompt: Your team is deploying a 70B-parameter LLM for inference, with ~10 ms latency budget per token. Walk through whether to deploy on GPU, TPU, or custom inference ASIC.
Explain in two or three sentences why specialized ML accelerators (TPU, NPU, AI ASIC) achieve 10-100× more ops-per-watt than general CPUs.
question.rubric: Mentions that specialization replaces flexible-but-expensive control logic (instruction fetch, decode, OoO, etc.) with simple data-flow patterns (systolic arrays, dot-product units); lower-precision arithmetic (FP16, FP8, INT8) shrinks energy per op; massive parallelism is exposed via dedicated structures. The cost is loss of generality — the accelerator only does one (or few) things well.
